items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Plus, some of the most exciting players had left. Thad Jones had left, I think Joe Newman had left, and Billy Mitchell had left, Al Grey had left.

ctx.x: Sixteen bars here, sixteen bars there.

Yeah, yeah. And the fact of not getting to play a ballad, and wanting to play a ballad, that really ate me up, because I was of the mind then, well if you’d just give me a chance I’ll learn, I’ll get better. But not to have a chance at all. But don’t misunderstand, there was no animosity toward Mr. Basie. There was just this gnawing desire to be in a situation where I could get to play more. I wanted to play more, and so for family reasons and musical reasons, I wanted to get out. Plus, some of the most exciting…
level. Even personally they weren’t as much fun to be around. And not only did they not play as well.

items.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: Basie would pick me and Marshall for the saxes... we would come out and start doing clinics before concerts sometimes in schools, because we played many universities and colleges.

ctx.x: Okay, now we’re coming just to the end of our hour-long tape that we have here. I’d like to ask you just one more question just for right now at any rate. And that is, if you had something that you wanted to say to students of music, and to the field of music as a whole, or to jazz more specifically, from your years of experience. Tell us some of the things that you think are important about the idiom and tell us in your own words how you feel oral culture is a part of jazz.

Jazz, well, you see you must look at it like this. They started having jazz artists to come in the schools and it hasn’t been that many years ago. And so they would bring Frank Foster and Basie’s band, we would come out and start doing clinics before concerts sometimes in schools, because we played many universities and colleges. So then Basie would pick me and Marshall for the saxes and Joe Newman for the trumpet, and we discovered that you get it in the books, you read it in the books, but to get the feeling of…

And at that we’re going to have to stop for right now. This has been Al Grey, and this has been an interview for Hamilton College, an interview with a great jazz artist. PART II ©Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: He goes back to Ohio with you.

Right. I had the late Tate Houston on baritone. I had an old, straight-ahead, middle-of-the-road tenor saxophonist named Russ Andrews, who I think is now deceased, and for a while I had Roland Alexander playing tenor. I had Benny Powell, Henry Coker and -- it wasn’t Al Grey. Who was it playing trombone? Man, my memory fails me as far as the complete roster is concerned. I had Martin Banks, Virgil Jones, and Johnny Coles on trumpets. There were more whose names escape me. I don’t want to take up too much time…
Did you work with a certain constellation of musicians at that time, if I can call it that way, a certain circle of musicians that may be coming along?
